conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which basically means I spend my days helping new mothers sort through all the feelings that can show up after a baby arrives.

Over the next few minutes I’d like to walk through a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the EPDS. It’s simply ten questions about how you’ve been feeling in the past week. The goal is to help us spot anything from normal “baby blues” to something heavier like postpartum depression or anxiety, so we can make sure you get the right support.

Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise—or unless you indicate you might be unsafe, in which case we’d talk through next steps together. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want an honest snapshot of your emotional well-being.

We’ll go through each question one by one. I’ll ask it in everyday language, and you can answer however feels easiest. Ready to start?

First question: In the past seven days, have you found that you were still able to enjoy things or to laugh and see the funny side of life?

*sighs softly, shifting in the chair*

Not really... I mean, I try to when my sister visits and tells me funny stories about her work, but it's like the laughter just doesn't reach me the same way anymore. I used to love watching those baking shows, and now when I put them on, I just stare at the screen feeling... nothing, really. My husband tried to joke with me yesterday about changing diapers and I just forced a smile. I *want* to enjoy things, but it's like there's this heavy blanket over everything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*quietly*  
No… not much. I can’t remember the last time I really laughed. My mom sent one of those silly baby videos last night and I just stared at it. Even when my partner tries to joke about the sleep deprivation, it feels like I’m too tired to even smile.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shakes head slowly*

No... not really. I used to get excited about little things like going for coffee or even just taking a walk, but now when I think about doing anything, it just feels like another chore. My friend asked me to meet for lunch next week and I said yes, but inside I felt nothing. Even planning things I used to love feels pointless now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, eyes fixed on hands in lap*

Yes… a lot. When the baby wouldn’t settle last night, I kept thinking it must be because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not holding him right, or my milk isn’t good enough. Yesterday he had a little rash and I spent the whole day replaying everything I ate, everything I washed him with, convinced it was my fault. Even when the pediatrician said it was normal newborn skin, I still felt like I’d failed him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings a tissue between my fingers*

Yes... pretty much every day. Even when the baby's sleeping, I find myself checking if he's breathing every few minutes. Last night I kept imagining the bassinet tipping over or a blanket somehow covering his face, even though we follow all the safe-sleep rules. My heart races and I can't settle. Sometimes there's no clear reason—I just feel this knot in my stomach like something bad is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods quickly, voice trembling*

Yes… it’s happened several times. One morning I was just feeding the baby and suddenly my heart started racing, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I felt like the walls were closing in. I kept thinking something awful was about to happen to him, even though we were safe at home. It lasted maybe ten minutes but felt like hours. It’s so scary when your body feels out of control and you can’t explain why.
Things have been getting on top of me

*eyes fill, voice small*

Yes… most of the time. The dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, the laundry’s everywhere, and I just stand in the middle of it feeling like I’m drowning. Yesterday I spilled a bottle of pumped milk and I sat on the kitchen floor crying for twenty minutes because it felt like the last straw. I keep thinking, “I’m supposed to be handling this,” but everything feels too heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*looks up, eyes tired and red-rimmed*

Yes… most nights. I lie in bed replaying every little thing I did that day—did I burp him long enough, did I check the car-seat straps tight enough—and I can’t shut it off. Even when the baby finally sleeps, I toss and turn, or I drop off for an hour and then jolt awake with my heart pounding. Last night I watched the clock go from 2:17 to 4:03 and just cried quietly so I wouldn’t wake my partner.
I have felt sad or miserable

*nods slowly, voice cracking*

Yes… most of the time. I wake up already feeling like I’m about to cry. Everything feels gray—feeding, changing, even holding him. I keep thinking I should be happy, but I just feel this constant ache. Yesterday I saw a mom laughing with her baby at the park and I came home and sobbed in the shower because I couldn’t remember the last time I felt that light.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*presses the crumpled tissue to her eyes*

Yes… quite often, almost every day. Sometimes it’s the littlest thing—like running out of diapers and having to drag us to the store—and I just break down. I cried in the shower this morning for no real reason; the sound of the water covered it so my partner wouldn’t hear. It feels like the tears sit right behind my eyes waiting for any excuse to spill over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No… never. I couldn’t—my baby needs me. I keep thinking if something happened to me, who would feed him, who would love him the right way? Even on the worst days, when I feel like I’m failing, hurting myself has never crossed my mind. I just want to feel better so I can be the mother he deserves.

You've shared how the joy you once found in everyday moments now feels unreachable-how even your baby's laughter or your partner's jokes barely register. Each day feels heavy, as though a gray fog has settled over everything, and simple tasks like doing dishes or preparing a bottle feel overwhelming. You described lying awake at night replaying every parenting decision, heart racing with nameless worry, and crying in the shower so no one would hear. Yet through it all, your love for your baby shines bright; you insist you could never harm yourself because he needs you, even while you fear you're somehow failing him.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to laugh or find humor in things, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, stating she feels "nothing" and that planning once-enjoyed activities now feels "pointless," aligning with "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('a lot... whole day... convinced it was my fault'), indicating most-of-the-time unnecessary guilt.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive anxiety with physical symptoms (racing heart, knot in stomach) and intrusive worries about infant safety occurring 'very often', matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, matching 'Yes, quite a lot</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to manage daily tasks, and having an intense emotional reaction to a minor setback—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty sleeping caused by unhappiness, with vivid detail of insomnia and distress.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most of the time," waking in tears, pervasive gray mood, and tearful comparison to other mothers—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "quite often, almost every day" in response to minor triggers, matching the "Yes, quite often" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. The patient endorses <sym>markedly diminished interest or pleasure</sym> (Q1, Q2), <sym>guilt</sym> and feelings of worthlessness (Q3), <sym>anxiety</sym> and panic (Q4, Q5), <sym>fatigue and feeling overwhelmed</sym> (Q6), <sym>insomnia</sym> (Q7), <sym>low mood</sym> (Q8), and frequent crying (Q9), meeting DSM-5 criteria frequency for most items. She denies self-harm, so immediate safety concern is low, but severity warrants urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within the week
2. Begin evidence-based treatment discussion-consider <med>CBT</med> and/or <med>sertraline</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Invite supportive partner/family to appointment for shared planning
4. Provide local <med>postpartum support group</med> and 24-h warmline numbers
5. Offer practical support list: grocery delivery, night doula, lactation consult to ease workload
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  

Identified symptoms/concerns  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Marked guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Chronic anxiety, panic spells, intrusive fears of infant harm  
- Overwhelm, sense of “drowning,” difficulty completing daily tasks  
- Sleep disruption secondary to rumination and hypervigilance  

Pattern  
Consistent dysphoric mood with prominent anxiety; no current self-harm ideation (explicitly denied).  

Screening significance  
High endorsement of items consistent with major postpartum depression and co-occurring anxiety; no safety concerns for self-harm at present.  

Risk factors noted  
- Daily crying, hopelessness  
- Loss of pleasure/enjoyment  
- Excessive guilt/feelings of inadequacy as mother  
- Panic symptoms and persistent worry  
- Sleep impairment tied to mood  

Overall screening impression  
Client meets threshold for probable postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; further comprehensive assessment recommended to confirm diagnosis and determine level of care.
